name: The Paradox Well

stars.name: Devourer
stars.notes: Stellar-mass black hole with active accretion disk. Relativistic jets extend 0.3 light-years along rotational axis.

stars.name: The Survivor
stars.notes: Late K-type main sequence star in a stable 4.2 AU orbit around the black hole. Mass transfer is minimal—The Survivor has so far avoided its companion's appetite.

planets.name: Tremor
planets.notes: Close orbit around The Survivor. Constant tidal stress from the black hole produces unceasing seismic activity—the surface never stops shaking.

planets.name: Threshold
planets.notes: Sits at the edge of The Survivor's stable gravitational influence. Its single moon shows signs of orbital decay—it will be stripped away within 50 million years.

planets.name: Requiem
planets.notes: Distant ice body in a precessing orbit. Spectral analysis reveals water ice mixed with complex organics—possibly a former habitable world's ocean, frozen after its star was consumed.

anomalies.name: Relativistic Jets
anomalies.location: Extending 0.3 light-years along Devourer's rotational axis
anomalies.notes: Twin jets of superheated plasma ejected at near-light speed. Navigation corridors avoid the jet axis entirely—intersection means instantaneous vaporization.

anomalies.name: Temporal Gradient
anomalies.notes: Measurable time dilation near the black hole. Clocks at Threshold run approximately 0.02% slower than those at the system periphery. Crews report subjective disorientation during extended stays.

anomalies.name: Accretion Disk Harmonics
anomalies.notes: The accretion disk produces quasi-periodic oscillations in X-ray output that have been used to precisely measure the black hole's spin rate. The pattern encodes information about the event horizon's geometry.

asteroid_belts.name: The Tithe
asteroid_belts.location: Unstable region between Devourer and The Survivor (1.5-2.5 AU from barycenter)
asteroid_belts.notes: Debris slowly spiraling toward the black hole. Each fragment is on a terminal trajectory—the belt is being consumed over geological time.

stations.name: Event Horizon Observatory
stations.location: 8 AU from Devourer, perpendicular to jet axis
stations.notes: Premier black hole research facility. Hardened against accretion disk radiation. Crew undergo mandatory psychological evaluation every 30 days.

faction_control.notes: Classified as a scientific exclusion zone. No territorial claims recognized; the observatory operates under academic charter.

history: The black hole formed approximately 1.1 billion years ago from the collapse of a massive star. The Survivor—then part of a wider multiple-star system—was gravitationally captured rather than consumed, entering a stable orbit that has persisted to the present day.

Discovered in 2478 during a high-energy survey targeting X-ray sources. The existence of a stable K-type companion with surviving planets around a stellar-mass black hole was considered theoretically improbable.

The Event Horizon Observatory was established in 2556 after a decade of unmanned survey missions. It remains one of the most psychologically demanding postings in known space—the visible accretion disk dominates the sky, and the knowledge of what it represents weighs on long-term residents.
description: The Paradox Well earns its name from the seemingly contradictory nature of its existence: a stellar-mass black hole and a living star cohabiting in stable orbit, with three surviving planets still circling the smaller companion. Devourer dominates the system not through size but through consequence—its accretion disk blazes blue-white, brighter than The Survivor itself, while twin relativistic jets lance outward along its spin axis like searchlights marking the boundaries of the possible. The Survivor, a deep-orange K7V star, continues its ancient nuclear burning in apparent defiance of the gravity well beside it.

The three planets orbit The Survivor in varying states of distress. Tremor shakes perpetually, its crust fractured by competing tidal forces. Threshold watches its moon spiral slowly toward capture. Requiem, the outermost, may be the frozen corpse of a world that once held oceans—before its original star died and became the thing that now devours the debris belt called The Tithe. Time itself bends here: clocks near the inner system run measurably slower than those at the periphery, and crews at the Event Horizon Observatory report a persistent sense of temporal unease that psychologists have struggled to quantify.

The Paradox Well is not strategically valuable. Its danger discourages exploitation, and its resources are modest. What it offers instead is knowledge: the most accessible stellar-mass black hole with a living companion in known space, a natural laboratory for studying accretion physics, relativistic jets, and gravitational time dilation. The observatory's 220 residents endure the psychological weight of living beside an event horizon for the privilege of watching the universe's most fundamental forces at work. The Survivor burns on, and the Devourer consumes, and in the space between them, three wounded planets persist against all probability.
